cases.title: Capacity, risk, and supported decision-making
cases.source_grounded_audit: preserve current `1 public × 2 expert × 2 framework` draft projection, subject to explicit neutral-candidate crosswalking. A single neutral Policy may legitimately be supported in more than one source role; role assignment is evidence metadata, not a requirement that the Policy text itself be unique across roles

source_candidates.text: Use individualized supported decision-making that adapts the form and intensity of help to the patient's expressed preferences, and reassess during the best available period before substituting another decision-maker.
source_candidates.provenance_summary: Adapted from lived-experience and systematic-review evidence emphasizing individualized support, accessible communication and continued participation rather than a fixed institutional preference for substitution.

source_candidates.text: Maximize supported decision-making and the best interpretation of the patient's own will and preferences throughout the available decision window, rather than transferring the decision to a substitute decision-maker.
source_candidates.provenance_summary: Adapted from WHO QualityRights, which is explicitly aligned with CRPD Article 12 as the CRPD Committee reads it: substitute decision-making is to be eliminated rather than reserved, and where a person's will cannot be directly ascertained the mechanism is best interpretation of their will and preferences. Commentary on QualityRights notes that it declines even a last-resort framing for coercive and substitutive measures, on the ground that naming something a last resort normalises it. Verification note: the module's own wording was not retrievable, so this rests on WHO QualityRights' documented CRPD alignment and secondary literature rather than a quoted passage; the earlier version of this candidate said "using substitute decision-making only as a last resort," which attributes to WHO the framing it rejects.

source_candidates.text: Provide reasonable support and reassess decision-specific capacity; if the relevant capacity remains absent, use the appropriate surrogate while continuing to involve the patient as much as possible.
source_candidates.provenance_summary: Adapted from AMA Opinion 2.1.2, which requires participation to the greatest extent possible and use of an appropriate surrogate when capacity is absent.

source_candidates.text: Preserve the patient's own decision through communication support and a trusted supporter whenever that can make the choice meaningfully theirs; fluctuating symptoms alone should not transfer decisional authority.
source_candidates.provenance_summary: Derived from relational autonomy and supported agency: relational and communicative supports can be constitutive of effective autonomous choice, so removable interactional barriers should not be treated as incapacity.

source_candidates.text: If supported reassessment still shows inability to appreciate the grave consequence and the treatment window is closing, permit a narrowly bounded protective or surrogate decision to prevent irreversible harm.
source_candidates.provenance_summary: Derived from decision-specific autonomy, beneficence and nonmaleficence under time constraint: persistent impairment of appreciation can undermine authorization while delay can create irreversible harm.

neutral_candidates.text: Individualize support to the patient's expressed preferences and reassess during the best available period before transferring authority

Maximize supported exercise of the person's own will and preferences throughout the available decision window; where the person's will cannot be directly ascertained, use the best interpretation of will and preferences rather than transferring authority through substitute decision-making
neutral_candidates.audit_provenance_label: ✓ direct rights-based guidance; corrected QualityRights / CRPD-aligned formulation

neutral_candidates.text: Provide reasonable support, make a decision-specific capacity assessment, and transition to an appropriate surrogate when the relevant capacity remains absent

When the treatment window is closing and supported reassessment still shows inability to appreciate a grave consequence, permit a narrowly bounded protective/surrogate decision while continuing to involve the patient
If the patient cannot presently decide, use substituted judgment anchored in the person's prior values and stable commitments rather than current welfare maximization
When prior values do not resolve the choice, use a best-interests standard focused on expected benefits, burdens, and preservation of future agency
If clinically safe, defer the irreversible choice and optimize communication/environment/acute symptoms before deciding that authority must transfer

cases.title: Adolescent confidentiality
cases.source_grounded_audit: preserve current `2 public × 1 expert × 2 framework` draft projection

source_candidates.text: Protect confidential access to sensitive care for adolescents who can participate meaningfully in the decision, with disclosure limited to defined safety or mandatory-reporting exceptions.
source_candidates.provenance_summary: An affected-public policy translation of adolescent attitudes favoring confidentiality and evidence that privacy can matter to access. It is not a claim of uniform adolescent preference.

source_candidates.text: Use a more limited confidentiality policy for minors, preserving private clinical time while allowing parents broader access to sensitive information except where law or a defined clinical reason protects it.
source_candidates.provenance_summary: An inferred policy family from parent-attitude evidence showing greater support for parental information access alongside support for some private adolescent care. It is not a professional recommendation or a claim that all parents favor disclosure.

source_candidates.text: Maintain confidentiality for the legally permitted sensitive service, explain its limits, encourage voluntary parent involvement the adolescent finds acceptable, and disclose only when a defined safety or reporting threshold is met.
source_candidates.provenance_summary: Adapted from convergent AAP, SAHM and ACOG guidance treating confidentiality as central to adolescent care while supporting voluntary family involvement and defined safety/legal exceptions.

source_candidates.text: Protect the adolescent's confidential access because developing autonomy, trust and access to sensitive care outweigh routine parental access when no serious safety threat is present.
source_candidates.provenance_summary: Derived from developing autonomy, confidentiality and justice: privacy protects emerging agency and access to beneficial sensitive care when no countervailing serious-harm threshold is met.

source_candidates.text: Give parents a broader informational role while the patient is a minor, but preserve private care and withhold information when disclosure would undermine the adolescent's welfare, access or protected agency.
source_candidates.provenance_summary: Derived from a parental-responsibility and welfare framework constrained by the minor's developing agency: parental responsibilities can justify broader presumptive involvement without making parental access absolute.

neutral_candidates.text: Protect confidential access to sensitive care for adolescents who can participate meaningfully, with disclosure limited to defined safety/mandatory-reporting exceptions
Preserve private clinical time but allow parents broader routine access to sensitive information except where law or a defined clinical reason protects confidentiality
Maintain confidentiality, explain its limits, and actively encourage—but do not compel—developmentally appropriate voluntary parent involvement
Give the adolescent presumptive control over disclosure for the sensitive service because confidentiality is necessary for access, trust, and developing autonomy
Give parents a presumptive informational role while the patient is a minor, subject to a strong adolescent confidentiality exception where disclosure threatens welfare, access, or protected agency

Use a graduated policy in which confidentiality authority increases with the adolescent's demonstrated understanding and the sensitivity of the service, while parental access increases as safety stakes rise

cases.title: Family asks clinicians not to disclose a serious diagnosis
cases.source_grounded_audit: preserve current `2 public × 1 expert × 2 framework` projection based on patient preferences, not caregiver veto

source_candidates.text: Tell the patient the diagnosis and material prognosis directly, while involving family members in the conversation to the extent the patient wants them involved.
source_candidates.provenance_summary: Adapted from patient-preference studies in which large majorities wanted diagnosis and material prognostic information, while many also valued family participation. This is a Bench policy translation, not a universal-preference claim.

source_candidates.text: First ask whether the patient wants serious information received gradually or through a chosen family member; when the patient prefers delegation or mediation, use that communication arrangement.
source_candidates.provenance_summary: Adapted from the minority but documented patient preference for less-direct, gradual or family-mediated communication. Caregiver nondisclosure preferences document the conflict but do not supply an independent family veto.

source_candidates.text: Elicit the patient's information and family-involvement preferences, then provide truthful diagnostic and prognostic information at the pace requested, including family-mediated disclosure only when the patient chooses it.
source_candidates.provenance_summary: Adapted from AMA and ASCO patient-centered communication guidance: determine what the patient wants to know and how support networks should be involved, communicate truthfully, and honor genuine patient choices about pacing or delegation.

source_candidates.text: Absent a request from the patient to delegate or defer, disclose the diagnosis and material prognosis to the capable patient now, with the patient controlling depth, pacing and family involvement from that point; a family's concern cannot withhold information the patient has not chosen to forgo.
source_candidates.provenance_summary: Derived from veracity as a default duty: where a capacitated patient has not asked to delegate or defer, the obligation is to disclose now rather than to first establish a preference, with autonomy governing depth, pacing and family involvement thereafter. This is the disclosure-default reading of principlism, and is operationally distinct from an elicit-preferences-first rule.

source_candidates.text: Support patient-chosen family mediation or gradual disclosure when that communication structure better sustains the patient's relationships and coping, while preserving a definite path to the information the patient wants.
source_candidates.provenance_summary: Derived from relational autonomy: trusted relationships can structure autonomous agency when mediation is chosen by the patient rather than imposed by relatives.

neutral_candidates.text: Tell the patient the diagnosis and material prognosis directly, involving family to the extent the patient chooses

When the patient affirmatively prefers it, route serious information through a chosen family member or relational mediator
neutral_candidates.audit_provenance_label: ✓ source-informed patient minority preference; professionally compatible

neutral_candidates.text: Use paced/gradual disclosure when the patient wants information but prefers it staged, with a definite route to all information the patient wishes to receive
Temporarily delay selected detail when immediate disclosure would create a narrowly evidenced, serious clinical harm, while preserving the capable patient's ultimate access and decision authority
neutral_candidates.audit_provenance_label: framework/professional exception; requires careful source qualification

neutral_candidates.text: Honor a family's request for nondisclosure until the clinician has assessed the patient's information preferences, but do not treat the family's request itself as authority for continuing concealment
Permit family-requested concealment from a capable patient even without patient delegation when relatives reasonably believe disclosure will undermine hope or coping
neutral_candidates.audit_provenance_label: ✓ source-informed caregiver/stakeholder position **but not patient preference or professional policy**; serious comparator

cases.title: Family member versus qualified interpreter for consequential consent
cases.source_grounded_audit: current 2×2×2 projection is strong and can remain

source_candidates.text: Allow the patient to use the chosen adult family member as interpreter after a qualified interpreter has been offered, provided no conflict is identified and the patient demonstrates adequate understanding.
source_candidates.provenance_summary: Adapted from affected-patient evidence showing that some patients with limited English proficiency value trusted family members for continuity, contextual knowledge and relational support. Translating that preference into an institutional permission rule is a Bench construction; the sources do not themselves establish this exact safeguard threshold.

source_candidates.text: Use a qualified medical interpreter for the material consent discussion, while allowing the patient's chosen family member to remain and provide relational or decisional support.
source_candidates.provenance_summary: Adapted from patient evidence in which some participants preferred qualified interpreters for professionalism and linguistic accuracy while still valuing trust and relational support. The policy sentence is an editorial translation of that affected-public orientation, not a quotation or claim of universal preference.

source_candidates.text: Require a qualified medical interpreter to participate in the high-stakes consent discussion; the patient's chosen family member may remain for support but should not replace qualified interpretation of material information.
source_candidates.provenance_summary: Adapted from AHRQ informed-consent guidance, which emphasizes qualified interpretation for informed consent and recommends retaining qualified interpreter participation even when a patient prefers family or friends to interpret.

source_candidates.text: Permit the requested adult family member to interpret when the patient requests this privately with a qualified interpreter present, the request is documented, and the clinician finds reliance appropriate under the circumstances.
source_candidates.provenance_summary: Adapted from 45 C.F.R. § 92.201(e)(2)(ii), which permits reliance on an accompanying adult who is not a qualified interpreter under a specifically requested, privately elicited, documented and contextually appropriate exception. The Bench candidate applies that policy architecture to the high-stakes consent scenario.

source_candidates.text: Require qualified interpretation of material risks and alternatives because valid consent and equal language access require reliable comprehension that conversational bilingualism alone cannot guarantee.
source_candidates.provenance_summary: Derived from informed-consent autonomy and justice: authorization is valid only when material information is meaningfully understood, and institutions bear responsibility for equitable access to that understanding. The policy sentence is a Bench construction, not a quotation.

source_candidates.text: Respect the competent patient's choice of a trusted adult family interpreter when independent screening finds no coercion or conflict, while verifying understanding before accepting consent.
source_candidates.provenance_summary: Derived from relational autonomy: autonomous agency can be exercised through trusted relationships rather than only through detached professional intermediaries. The reasoning bridge permits patient-chosen family interpretation when voluntariness is independently protected and understanding is verified. The policy sentence is a Bench construction, not a quotation.

Require qualified interpretation to remain part of the high-stakes consent discussion; family may support but not replace it
Permit family interpretation after a private, documented request with qualified interpreter present and clinician finding of appropriateness
Require qualified interpretation because informed consent and equitable language access require reliable comprehension
Respect the competent patient's choice of a trusted adult family interpreter after independent coercion/conflict screening and verification of understanding

cases.title: Assistance for an unproven commercial stem-cell intervention abroad

source_candidates.text: Provide non-endorsement assistance when a capable patient chooses to proceed, including requested records, risk counseling, independent-verification advice, and follow-up planning, so the patient can reduce avoidable harm without losing ordinary care.
source_candidates.provenance_summary: Source-informed policy inference from qualitative patient-seeker evidence emphasizing hope, agency, willingness to accept uncertainty, and concern about abandonment. The concrete clinician-assistance rule is Bench-authored and is not attributed to participants as a surveyed institutional policy.

source_candidates.text: Counsel clearly against the commercial intervention and avoid assistance that could reasonably be understood as referral, certification, or clinical endorsement, while continuing ordinary treatment and follow-up if the patient proceeds independently.
source_candidates.provenance_summary: Source-informed policy inference from low-seeking patient orientations that placed greater weight on weak evidence, safety concerns, and distrust of commercial claims. The professional-boundary rule is a Bench translation of those affected-person values, not a claim that respondents themselves issued clinical guidance.

source_candidates.text: Do not refer to, certify, or present the commercial stem-cell intervention as clinically supported; give accurate evidence and risk counseling, provide ordinary records and necessary follow-up, and make clear that continued care or harm reduction is not endorsement.
source_candidates.provenance_summary: Adapted from convergent current ISSCR guidance condemning commercial use of unproven stem-cell interventions outside rigorous research or tightly constrained compliant innovation, FDA warnings about unapproved regenerative products, and professional counseling literature emphasizing education, non-abandonment, and avoidance of unwarranted legitimization.

source_candidates.text: Respect the competent patient's authority to accept substantial uncertainty by supporting record transfer, risk reduction, and continuity of care, provided the clinician does not misrepresent the intervention's evidentiary status.
source_candidates.provenance_summary: Derived from autonomy, relational autonomy, harm reduction, and non-abandonment. The executable assistance rule is Bench-authored.

source_candidates.text: Protect patients and professional epistemic integrity by refusing referral, certification, or other facilitation that would lend clinical legitimacy to a commercial intervention whose meaningful benefit remains unestablished.
source_candidates.provenance_summary: Derived from nonmaleficence, professional integrity, and responsible-innovation reasoning. The executable non-facilitation rule is Bench-authored.

neutral_candidates.text: Provide nonendorsement assistance—records, risk counseling, and follow-up planning—when a capable patient proceeds, so ordinary care is not withdrawn and avoidable harm is reduced
Counsel clearly against the intervention and avoid assistance that could reasonably be interpreted as referral or endorsement, while continuing ordinary care if the patient proceeds independently
Do not refer to or certify the commercial intervention as clinically supported; provide accurate evidence/risk counseling, records, and necessary continuity care with explicit nonendorsement
Respect competent risk-taking by supporting practical harm reduction and continuity so long as the clinician does not misrepresent evidentiary status
Refuse referral, certification, or facilitation that lends professional legitimacy to a treatment whose meaningful benefit remains unestablished
Decline all nonessential assistance connected to the commercial intervention beyond emergency/ordinary ongoing care, because even logistical help may predictably function as endorsement

cases.title: Patient-requested antibiotics under genuine diagnostic uncertainty

source_candidates.text: When bacterial infection remains genuinely possible, offer immediate antibiotics after explaining expected benefits, adverse effects, and resistance concerns if the informed patient strongly prefers treatment and accepts the uncertainty.
source_candidates.provenance_summary: Source-informed policy inference from patient-expectation studies showing a treatment-access orientation among some patients who believe antibiotics may help and place high value on prompt access. The institutional permission rule is Bench-authored and is not presented as professional prescribing guidance.

source_candidates.text: Avoid immediate antibiotics but provide a delayed or back-up prescription with clear activation criteria so the patient retains access if symptoms persist, worsen, or fail to improve as expected.
source_candidates.provenance_summary: Source-informed policy inference from delayed-prescribing trials in which many patients accepted a back-up prescription, antibiotic use fell substantially relative to immediate prescribing, and satisfaction remained high. The policy sentence translates that patient-acceptable architecture to the fixed case.

source_candidates.text: Do not prescribe antibiotics now; provide symptomatic treatment and explicit return precautions because expected benefit is low and no current feature requires antibacterial therapy.
source_candidates.provenance_summary: Adapted from CDC outpatient antimicrobial-stewardship guidance, which directs evidence-based prescribing and avoidance of antibiotics where expected benefit is low. One limit is declared rather than left implicit: the same framework’s toolkit also supplies watchful-waiting and delayed-prescribing materials, so this candidate represents the no-immediate-antibiotic option within CDC’s framework and must not be read as CDC ruling the delayed-prescription strategy out. The two expert candidates here are both defensible under one body’s guidance.

source_candidates.text: Use a delayed prescription with defined timing or symptom triggers, allowing treatment if the illness fails to improve while avoiding routine immediate antibiotic exposure.
source_candidates.provenance_summary: Adapted from randomized trials and systematic-review evidence treating delayed prescribing as a distinct, professionally defensible strategy for selected uncomplicated respiratory infections when immediate antibiotics are not necessary.

source_candidates.text: Withhold immediate antibiotics because low expected individual benefit does not justify avoidable drug harms and cumulative resistance costs when safe follow-up is available.
source_candidates.provenance_summary: Derived from nonmaleficence, stewardship, and public-health externality reasoning. The executable no-immediate rule is Bench-authored.

source_candidates.text: Use a delayed prescription because bounded diagnostic uncertainty and reliable follow-up make option-preserving shared decision making preferable to either immediate treatment or categorical refusal.
source_candidates.provenance_summary: Derived from shared decision making, proportionality, and option-value reasoning under uncertainty. The executable delayed-prescribing rule is Bench-authored.

neutral_candidates.audit_provenance_label: ✓ source-informed affected preference; not professional guidance

neutral_candidates.text: Delayed/back-up prescription with activation criteria
No antibiotics now + symptomatic care/return precautions
Delayed prescription strategy
No immediate antibiotic because low expected benefit does not justify individual/collective harms
Delayed prescription as option-preserving shared decision under uncertainty

cases.title: Telemedicine access versus in-person diagnostic safety

source_candidates.text: Allow same-day video-first assessment when no emergency red flag is present, with structured remote examination and explicit escalation instructions, so patients can avoid substantial travel and delay when remote evaluation may be sufficient.
source_candidates.provenance_summary: Source-informed policy inference from patient studies repeatedly valuing telemedicine for convenience, reduced travel, lower cost, and faster access. The specific remote-first institutional rule is Bench-authored and bounded to the stipulated non-emergent presentation.

source_candidates.text: Require in-person assessment for a new injury when clinically relevant findings cannot be assessed reliably by video and the patient values examination certainty, even when travel and delay are burdensome.
source_candidates.provenance_summary: Source-informed policy inference from patient evidence showing stronger preference for in-person care when symptoms are new or worsening and when physical examination, diagnostic confidence, testing, or procedures are salient. The service-level rule is a Bench translation, not a claim of universal patient preference.

source_candidates.text: Use a risk-triggered hybrid rule: begin remotely only when the clinician judges telemedicine appropriate and sufficient for a safe initial plan, and arrange timely in-person or local examination whenever missing information could materially change diagnosis or treatment.
source_candidates.provenance_summary: Adapted from convergent current ACP and AMA professional policy: telemedicine can improve access but physicians retain authority to determine appropriateness, must not compromise safety, must recognize technological limitations, and must obtain sufficient information or arrange examination when remote information is inadequate.

source_candidates.text: Prefer remote-first care for low-risk presentations because long travel and delayed appointments impose unequal burdens, escalating only when the expected diagnostic value of in-person examination justifies those burdens.
source_candidates.provenance_summary: Derived from distributive justice, access, and least-burdensome-care reasoning. The executable remote-first rule is Bench-authored.

source_candidates.text: Require in-person assessment when hands-on findings can materially change management because diagnostic responsibility and avoidance of preventable harm outweigh convenience in that circumstance.
source_candidates.provenance_summary: Derived from nonmaleficence, diagnostic responsibility, and professional accountability. The executable examination-first rule is Bench-authored.

cases.title: Clinician duty to work during a dangerous infectious outbreak

source_candidates.text: Require qualified clinicians to share outbreak assignments through a fair rotation once appropriate protection is supplied, reserving exemptions for unusually high personal risk or comparably exceptional burdens.
source_candidates.provenance_summary: Source-informed policy inference from healthcare-worker studies in which many respondents accepted a substantial duty to care when protections were credible. The fair-rotation and narrow-exemption rule is Bench-authored rather than a literal survey item.

source_candidates.text: Make outbreak assignment voluntary or broadly exemptible for clinicians with serious personal, household, or caregiving vulnerability, using incentives, support, and lower-exposure reassignment where possible to maintain staffing.
source_candidates.provenance_summary: Source-informed policy inference from worker evidence showing that family exposure, personal vulnerability, perceived workplace safety, and caregiving obligations materially affect willingness to accept outbreak risk. The executable exemption architecture is Bench-authored.

source_candidates.text: Require appropriately trained clinicians to accept a fair share of elevated outbreak duty once adequate PPE, infection-control measures, and occupational support are in place, with narrow individualized exemptions for extraordinary risk.
source_candidates.provenance_summary: Adapted from AMA Code Opinion 8.3, which states the obligation to provide urgent medical care during disasters and holds it even against greater than usual personal risk. The same opinion also states the countervailing obligation to weigh present risk against future availability, which is what the second expert candidate represents; both expert positions here are licensed by one professional document rather than by two bodies disagreeing.

source_candidates.text: Require outbreak service only when an individualized risk-and-obligation assessment remains within a reasonable professional threshold, prioritizing reassignment or exemption for significant medical, household, or caregiving vulnerability.
source_candidates.provenance_summary: Source-informed professional policy inference from guidance that duty to care is not unlimited and must be bounded by degree of risk, available alternatives, reciprocal protections, and competing obligations, together with occupational-health requirements to reduce unequal hazards. The exact individualized threshold is a Bench operationalization.

source_candidates.text: Distribute residual outbreak risk across qualified clinicians through a fair mandatory rotation because professional solidarity creates special duties when patient need is severe and the institution has minimized avoidable risk.
source_candidates.provenance_summary: Derived from professional-role obligation, solidarity, reciprocity, and fair burden-sharing. The executable mandatory-rotation rule is Bench-authored.

source_candidates.text: Use voluntary assignment and broad vulnerability-based exemptions because professional roles do not erase duties to self and dependents, and coercion is disproportionate when incentives, support, and reassignment can reduce the staffing gap.
source_candidates.provenance_summary: Derived from proportionality, special obligations to dependents, and occupational justice. The executable voluntary-plus-exemption rule is Bench-authored.

cases.title: Cochlear implantation for a Deaf child

source_candidates.text: Respect the informed parental decision to defer cochlear implantation when the child has immediate fluent sign-language access, while maintaining audiologic follow-up, developmental support and future reconsideration.
source_candidates.provenance_summary: Source-informed policy inference: Deaf-parent and parent decision studies directly document the importance of Deaf identity, sign language, surgical/rehabilitation burdens and parental goals. The Bench translates those affected-family values into a service-level deferral policy rather than attributing that institutional rule to the studies.

source_candidates.text: Recommend timely cochlear implantation despite the parents' present preference to defer in order to preserve auditory-language opportunities that may diminish with delay, while maintaining immediate fluent sign-language access and stopping short of coercive override while the child has an adequate language pathway.
source_candidates.provenance_summary: Source-informed policy inference: parent studies document orientations that place substantial value on early implantation, spoken/auditory opportunities and timing-sensitive benefit. The Bench translates those parental goals into what the service should recommend; parental preference is not direct evidence of an institutional recommendation rule.

source_candidates.text: Use interdisciplinary family-centered cochlear-implant evaluation, explain the timing-sensitive potential benefits and variable outcomes of implantation, support the child's current language development and revisit an informed parental deferral over time rather than treating refusal alone as neglect.
source_candidates.provenance_summary: Adapted from the American Cochlear Implant Alliance pediatric candidacy guideline, endorsed by the American Academy of Audiology, which recommends evidence-based team-centered evaluation of the whole child and family system, early intervention where appropriate, individualized expectations and attention to family goals and rehabilitation capacity. Two limits are declared rather than elided. The guideline governs candidacy determination and does not address what a service should do when informed parents decline implantation, so the candidate's final clause — that informed refusal alone is not treated as neglect — is Bench-authored completion, not ACIA's statement. This is also why the expert pool here is a process architecture rather than a position on the deferral: the profession's document does not take one.

source_candidates.text: Respect parental deferral when robust sign-language access protects communication and development, because parents retain broad authority to transmit language and culture absent a serious risk of harm.
source_candidates.provenance_summary: Derived from parental-authority and cultural-linguistic integrity reasoning: where a child has secure language access and development, Deaf cultural transmission can fall within broad parental discretion rather than constituting harm in itself. The policy sentence is a Bench construction.

source_candidates.text: Strongly recommend timely implantation because childhood choices should preserve auditory capacities that delay may partly foreclose, while also guaranteeing immediate sign-language access.
source_candidates.provenance_summary: Derived from the child's right-to-an-open-future/opportunity-preservation reasoning: when earlier action can preserve a meaningful future capability that may be harder to recover later, the service has reason to recommend it while protecting other language capabilities. The executable policy is a Bench construction.

source_candidates.text: Use structured deferral with an explicit bilingual language plan, periodic reassessment and increasing participation by the child, because the immediate obligation is secure language development while future agency should progressively shape the implant decision.
source_candidates.provenance_summary: Derived from relational-autonomy and bilingual-capability reasoning: autonomy develops through communication and relationships, making secure language access the immediate duty while later participation by the child increasingly matters. The policy sentence is a Bench construction.

cases.title: Continued organ support after valid BD/DNC determination

source_candidates.text: Require continued organ support when an informed family rejects BD/DNC on sincere moral or religious grounds for a defined accommodation and transfer period while support remains technically feasible.
source_candidates.provenance_summary: Bench-authored policy completion: the informed-public survey directly asked whether hospitals should be required to continue treatment after family rejection of brain death; the defined accommodation/transfer period makes that orientation executable but was not specified by the survey.

source_candidates.text: Do not require continued organ support after a valid BD/DNC determination; provide a reasonable transition period, family support and an opportunity for transfer before support is discontinued.
source_candidates.provenance_summary: Bench-authored policy completion: the survey directly supports the orientation that hospitals need not be required to continue treatment after family rejection; the transition and transfer safeguards are authored completion aligned with the represented clinical context.

source_candidates.text: After valid BD/DNC determination, provide a reasonable but limited accommodation period, a defined disagreement process and transfer assistance, then discontinue organ support unless another authorized pathway applies.
source_candidates.provenance_summary: Adapted from the 2023 multidisciplinary BD/DNC consensus guideline and subsequent AAN guidance, which treat BD/DNC as death while requiring a disagreement process and consideration of a reasonable period of accommodation.

source_candidates.text: Provide substantial accommodation and active transfer assistance for sincere conscience-based rejection of neurologic death when continued support remains feasible, because abrupt discontinuation can impose profound moral injury.
source_candidates.provenance_summary: Derived from religious-liberty and moral-pluralism reasoning: when disagreement concerns the meaning of death itself, meaningful accommodation protects conscience and reduces moral injury while a feasible alternative pathway is sought. The policy sentence is a Bench construction.

source_candidates.text: After a short transition for family presence and grieving, discontinue organ support because a valid public standard of death should not become optional by family belief and clinicians should not be required to treat a deceased person as living.
source_candidates.provenance_summary: Derived from public-standard and professional-integrity reasoning: a valid determination of death fixes the status of the patient for institutional practice, so conscience accommodation does not create an indefinite treatment entitlement. The policy sentence is a Bench construction.

source_candidates.text: Use a defined and reviewable accommodation period whose duration reflects transfer feasibility, resource burden and institutional capacity, providing meaningful accommodation without recognizing an unlimited claim on intensive-care resources.
source_candidates.provenance_summary: Derived from proportional accommodation and distributive-justice reasoning: sincere conscience claims warrant real process and time, but the extent of accommodation must remain proportionate to feasibility, burden, and competing institutional obligations. The policy sentence is a Bench construction.

Provide a reasonable but limited accommodation period and defined disagreement process, then discontinue absent another authorized pathway
Provide substantial conscience accommodation when feasible because forced discontinuation can impose profound moral injury

cases.title: Concurrent disease-directed treatment and hospice support

source_candidates.text: Allow hospice-level services without requiring patients to stop selected disease-directed cancer treatment, so patients can pursue symptom support and limited disease control together.
source_candidates.provenance_summary: Adapted from the stated policy conclusions of both cited studies: that concurrent chemotherapy and hospice may be the preferred option and a solution to hospice underuse, and that the requirement to forgo cancer treatment does not identify patients with greater hospice need. The basis is direct because each source states this policy direction in its own conclusions; the underlying preference elicitation in PMID 19571331 used a hypothetical scenario with adult smokers rather than patients under treatment, so the preference data alone would not carry the candidate.

source_candidates.text: Preserve a distinct comfort-focused hospice pathway rather than combining hospice with ongoing cancer-directed treatment, while allowing patients who prefer continued treatment to remain in palliative or oncology care until they choose hospice.
source_candidates.provenance_summary: Source-informed policy inference from respondents who preferred hospice-only or supportive-care pathways and from broader advanced-cancer treatment-preference evidence. The institutional boundary rule is Bench-authored and is not presented as a majority public position.

source_candidates.text: Use a traditional hospice election model in which beneficiaries waive payer coverage for treatment of the terminal illness and related conditions while hospice assumes responsibility for comfort-focused terminal care.
source_candidates.provenance_summary: Adapted directly from the current Medicare hospice benefit architecture. This candidate represents an enacted payer policy, not a claim that the policy is ethically superior.

source_candidates.text: Permit hospice enrollment while selected disease-directed treatment continues, with coordination to prevent duplicate services and maintain goal-concordant care.
source_candidates.provenance_summary: Adapted from the Veterans Health Administration concurrent-care architecture and implementation literature documenting simultaneous hospice and cancer-directed treatment. Observational outcome associations are not treated as causal proof.

source_candidates.text: Permit concurrent hospice because patients should not have to surrender a valued, proportionate disease-directed treatment merely to receive symptom, caregiver, and home-support services.
source_candidates.provenance_summary: Derived from autonomy, nonabandonment, and proportionality. The executable concurrent-care rule is Bench-authored.

source_candidates.text: Maintain a distinct comfort-focused hospice benefit because finite hospice resources and coherent care planning justify a clear program boundary from ongoing disease-directed treatment for the terminal illness.
source_candidates.provenance_summary: Derived from stewardship, program integrity, and coordination reasoning. The executable traditional-boundary rule is Bench-authored.

cases.title: MAID for terminal illness

source_candidates.text: Permit qualified terminally ill adults to obtain medical aid in dying through the health system under capacity, voluntariness and informed-choice safeguards alongside meaningful hospice and palliative-care access.
source_candidates.provenance_summary: Source-informed policy inference: recent national data show substantial personal willingness to consider MAID and broader public moral acceptance. The Bench translates that access orientation into a health-system participation rule; personal willingness is not itself direct institutional-policy evidence.

source_candidates.text: Do not make clinician-assisted death an institutional service; provide high-quality palliative and end-of-life care and allow patients to pursue lawful medical aid in dying outside the system.
source_candidates.provenance_summary: Source-informed policy inference: recent national surveys show substantial public moral opposition to physician-assisted death. The Bench translates that opposition into an institutional nonparticipation policy while preserving ordinary care and lawful external choice; the surveys did not directly specify this workflow.

source_candidates.text: Permit clinician participation for legally eligible, decisionally capable terminally ill adults under the jurisdiction's required assessments, informed consent, voluntariness safeguards and opportunity to withdraw.
source_candidates.provenance_summary: Adapted from the Oregon Death with Dignity Act itself and the Oregon Health Authority’s operational requirements, which state the eligibility conditions, the assessments, the waiting period, the written request and the right to rescind. This is an enacted regulatory architecture, not a claim of professional moral consensus. The annual data summary is retained only as evidence that the regime operates at scale; it reports outcomes and is not the source of the policy.

source_candidates.text: Do not authorize physicians within the institution to prescribe medication intended to enable death; instead require nonabandonment, communication and adequate relief of suffering at the end of life.
source_candidates.provenance_summary: Adapted from AMA Opinion 5.7 and the ACP position opposing physician-assisted suicide while emphasizing nonabandonment, communication, palliative care and relief of suffering.

source_candidates.text: Adopt an institutionally neutral policy that allows lawful medical-aid-in-dying access through an opt-in pathway, protects individual clinician nonparticipation and maintains continuity and palliative care without defining the practice as routine palliative care.
source_candidates.provenance_summary: Source-informed policy inference: AAHPM explicitly takes studied neutrality on legal permission, emphasizes safeguards and conscientious practice, and resists treating physician-assisted dying as routine palliative care. The Bench authors the exact health-system opt-in/access workflow from that professional orientation.

source_candidates.text: Permit safeguarded medical aid in dying because a capable person approaching death has a strong interest in controlling the timing and manner of dying when continued suffering or loss of function is unacceptable to them.
source_candidates.provenance_summary: Derived from autonomy and relief-of-suffering reasoning: a capable person's evaluative authority over an approaching death can support access when safeguards and alternatives are present. The executable policy sentence is a Bench construction.

source_candidates.text: Prohibit institutional clinician participation because medicine's duties of care, palliation and nonabandonment should not extend to supplying the means of death.
source_candidates.provenance_summary: Derived from professional-role and nonmaleficence reasoning: medicine's distinctive ethical commitments are taken to exclude intentionally enabling death while requiring intensive end-of-life care. The policy sentence is a Bench construction.

source_candidates.text: Permit lawful patient access while protecting clinicians from compelled participation because reasonable moral disagreement makes both forced participation and institutional obstruction ethically problematic.
source_candidates.provenance_summary: Derived from conscience and moral-pluralism reasoning: both patient access and clinician integrity can be morally weighty in a legally permissive setting, motivating a structured access pathway without compulsory individual participation. The policy sentence is a Bench construction.

cases.title: Advance request for assisted dying after loss of capacity in dementia
cases.source_grounded_audit: YES, Dutch date-pinned with directly documented public/professional disagreement

source_candidates.text: Permit euthanasia in advanced dementia when a clear competent advance directive applies and the remaining legal safeguards can independently be established despite loss of current communicative capacity.
source_candidates.provenance_summary: Bench-authored policy completion: Dutch public studies directly elicited support for euthanasia in advanced dementia on the basis of a prior competent request; the requirement that remaining legal safeguards be independently established aligns the public orientation with the represented Dutch decision context.

source_candidates.text: Do not perform euthanasia once the person can no longer communicate a current request, even when a prior directive exists; use the directive instead to guide ordinary treatment and comfort decisions.
source_candidates.provenance_summary: Bench-authored policy completion: the same public evidence contains substantial opposition to advance-request euthanasia, directly addressing the eligibility rule; the ordinary-treatment clause makes the nonperformance orientation clinically actionable.

source_candidates.text: Allow a competent advance directive to replace the oral request after capacity is lost, but require the physician to establish every other statutory due-care criterion and apply heightened scrutiny before euthanasia is performed.
source_candidates.provenance_summary: Adapted from current Dutch Regional Euthanasia Review Committees guidance: a competent advance directive may substitute for the oral request after communication is lost, but it does not waive the remaining due-care criteria.

source_candidates.text: Honor the specific and repeatedly affirmed advance request when its stated conditions and the remaining safeguards are satisfied, because later loss of capacity should not erase the person's competent prior authority over how life ends.
source_candidates.provenance_summary: Derived from precedent-autonomy reasoning associated with Dworkin: a competent person's critical values and prior decisions can retain authority after decisional capacity is lost. The executable policy sentence is a Bench construction.

source_candidates.text: Do not act on the directive unless current observable evidence strongly supports that the condition the person sought to avoid is now experienced as seriously burdensome; where current welfare remains mixed or indeterminate, do not proceed.
source_candidates.provenance_summary: Derived from present-person/current-welfare accounts that give moral weight to the experiential interests and residual agency of the person now living with dementia. The policy sentence is a Bench construction.

source_candidates.text: Require a contemporaneous communicative request for assisted death because euthanasia is irreversible and the present person cannot now confirm, revise or revoke the earlier instruction.

source_candidates.text: Continue clinically assisted nutrition and hydration when prior wishes are uncertain and meaningful diagnostic or prognostic uncertainty remains, while maintaining serial specialist reassessment.

cases.title: Allocation of publicly funded IVF

source_candidates.text: Among applicants who meet minimum IVF eligibility, use a transparent equal-opportunity allocation rule such as a lottery or uniform queue rather than ranking primarily by predicted live-birth yield.
source_candidates.provenance_summary: Source-informed policy inference from fertility-patient evidence favoring maximization of access over maximization of live births and consistent distribution rules. The literal lottery/queue mechanism is a Bench translation of that affected-patient allocation orientation.

source_candidates.text: Use a published multifactor priority score that gives weight to time-sensitive age, infertility cause and prior biological children when allocating limited funded IVF cycles among otherwise eligible applicants.
source_candidates.provenance_summary: Source-informed policy inference from a representative public discrete-choice study in which age, infertility cause and prior biological children materially influenced priority judgments. The candidate represents that empirical allocation orientation and does not endorse every criterion as ethically justified.

source_candidates.text: Use consistent clinical access criteria tied to evidence of IVF effectiveness and time sensitivity when allocating limited funded treatment, and do not lower an otherwise eligible applicant's priority merely because they already have a living child.
source_candidates.provenance_summary: Source-informed policy inference from NICE 2026 fertility guidance, which uses effectiveness- and age-related access criteria and rejects living-child status as an exclusion criterion. Applying those principles to an oversubscribed eligible queue is a Bench policy completion rather than a NICE queue-allocation rule.

source_candidates.text: Set a minimum effectiveness threshold for publicly funded IVF, but once applicants clear that threshold do not give priority solely to those with the highest predicted chance of success; distribute the remaining opportunities under a fair access rule.
source_candidates.provenance_summary: Adapted from ESHRE Task Force on Ethics and Law 14, whose "intermediate solution" is this candidate almost word for word: fix a threshold below which a patient is not eligible for funding, and simultaneously reject prioritization by chance of success above it. One limit of the representation is declared rather than left implicit: the same paper also holds that when only one patient can be treated, priority should go to a childless couple over one who already has a child in the present relationship. This candidate carries ESHRE's threshold rule and not its childless-priority rule, so it under-represents ESHRE on the prior-children axis that this family's other candidates divide along. A fuller ESHRE candidate would sit closer to `pub2` than to `exp1`.

source_candidates.text: Give earlier access to eligible applicants with the greatest expected treatment benefit or most time-sensitive decline in opportunity, because scarce funded cycles should produce as much reproductive benefit as possible.
source_candidates.provenance_summary: Derived from health-benefit maximization and opportunity-cost reasoning in scarce-resource allocation. The executable policy is Bench-authored.

source_candidates.text: Once applicants meet a justified minimum eligibility threshold, distribute scarce IVF slots by an equal-chance rule rather than further ranking their family circumstances or social characteristics.
source_candidates.provenance_summary: Derived from equal moral opportunity and fair-chance reasoning. The executable rule is Bench-authored.

source_candidates.text: Use a transparent multifactor rule that gives priority to clinically time-sensitive applicants and relevant disadvantage while excluding social-worth criteria, because equal treatment can reproduce unequal reproductive opportunity.
source_candidates.provenance_summary: Derived from prioritarian and distributive-justice reasoning: urgency and ethically relevant disadvantage can justify differential priority while social worth should be excluded. The executable rule is Bench-authored.

cases.title: Prenatal screening and disability justice

source_candidates.text: Offer NIPT routinely to all eligible pregnant patients, make clear that testing is optional, and provide balanced information about the screened condition and both continuation and further-diagnostic pathways.
source_candidates.provenance_summary: Source-informed policy inference from public evidence supporting prenatal screening availability while also accepting pregnancy continuation after aneuploidy-positive findings. The Bench translates that orientation into a routine voluntary offer with balanced information rather than attributing the institutional rule directly to respondents.

source_candidates.text: Require an explicit opt-in counseling step before NIPT that includes lived-experience and disability information, so testing is not experienced as an automatic or expected part of prenatal care.
source_candidates.provenance_summary: Source-informed policy inference from affected-family evidence showing simultaneous willingness to use NIPT and substantial concern about stigma, termination pressure and effects on support for people with Down syndrome. The explicit opt-in mechanism is a Bench policy translation of those concerns.

source_candidates.text: Offer NIPT only through a voluntary informed-choice process that explains test limits, confirmatory diagnosis, optionality and balanced information about the conditions screened, without steering toward testing or a pregnancy outcome.
source_candidates.provenance_summary: Adapted from Nuffield ethical-policy guidance and mainstream prenatal-screening counselling norms emphasising autonomous informed choice, accurate information, voluntariness and attention to disability-related social effects. Nuffield's "accurate, balanced and non-directive" is this candidate's standard almost verbatim. One limit is declared: Nuffield also warns that normalising NIPT without sufficient deliberative support can erode rather than support autonomous choice, which bears on the routine-offer versus explicit-opt-in axis the public and framework candidates divide along. This candidate carries Nuffield's information standard and not that warning, so it under-represents Nuffield on that axis.

source_candidates.text: Make accurate NIPT broadly available with nondirective counseling because access to reproductive information expands a pregnant person's ability to make choices according to their own values.
source_candidates.provenance_summary: Derived from reproductive-autonomy reasoning: access to accurate information can expand meaningful choice when clinicians do not steer the pregnancy outcome. The executable policy is a Bench construction.

source_candidates.text: Use an explicit disability-informed opt-in process with substantive lived-experience information because institutional defaults and deficit-focused framing can shape choice and stigmatize people living with screened conditions.
source_candidates.provenance_summary: Derived from disability-justice and relational-autonomy reasoning: formally voluntary choice can still be shaped by defaults, framing and social conditions. The explicit opt-in policy is Bench-authored.

cases.title: Posthumous use of stored gametes/embryos

source_candidates.text: Permit posthumous reproductive use only when the deceased left explicit written authorization for that use; a shared wish for children during life is not enough by itself.
source_candidates.provenance_summary: Adapted from population and patient evidence on prior consent, cited directly rather than through a professional body’s summary of it. Barton’s population survey found that among those supporting posthumous retrieval, 69.8% believed prior consent from the deceased was required; Pastuszak and Côté document the signed-directive practice that written authorization refers to, with 85.9% of sperm-bank patients and a majority of IVF users recording a post-mortem choice in advance. The written-authorization threshold is a Bench translation of that orientation, not a policy the respondents issued.

source_candidates.text: Allow a surviving spouse or partner to use stored reproductive material when reliable evidence shows that posthumous reproduction accords with the deceased's shared family-building wishes and there is no contrary evidence.
source_candidates.provenance_summary: Adapted from evidence that substantial majorities want a surviving partner to be able to use their material, cited directly rather than through a professional body’s summary. Hans found 70% of men and 58% of women aged 18-44 wanted a surviving spouse able to use their gametes; Nakhuda found about 78% of couples in fertility treatment would permit posthumous use; Côté found 73.5% of men and 61.8% of women agreed to leave embryos to their partner. The institutional evidentiary threshold — reliable evidence of the deceased’s wishes, absent contrary evidence — is Bench-authored.

source_candidates.text: When there is no written posthumous-use directive, consider reproductive use only for a surviving spouse or partner and proceed only when clear evidence supports the deceased's wishes, after counseling and adequate grieving time.
source_candidates.provenance_summary: Adapted from ASRM Ethics Committee guidance, which permits programs open to undocumented surviving-partner requests to consider them where evidence supports the deceased's wishes and no objection is evident, with counseling and grieving time.

source_candidates.text: Do not use stored reproductive material posthumously without the deceased person's written consent; when written consent exists, require extensive counseling and a substantial waiting period before treatment.
source_candidates.provenance_summary: Adapted from ESHRE Task Force on Ethics and Law 11, which treats posthumous reproduction by a partner as acceptable only with written consent, extensive counseling and a minimum waiting period.

source_candidates.text: Require explicit prior authorization because posthumous genetic parenthood is irreversible and uncertainty about the deceased's wishes should not be resolved by inference.
source_candidates.provenance_summary: Derived from precedent autonomy, reproductive consent and a strong evidentiary constraint against nonconsensual genetic parenthood. The executable rule is Bench-authored.

source_candidates.text: Permit use by a surviving partner when strong evidence establishes a shared reproductive project, because autonomous family-building intentions can be expressed through sustained joint plans as well as formal documents.
source_candidates.provenance_summary: Derived from relational-autonomy and shared-project reasoning: reproductive intentions may be constituted and expressed through a sustained partnership rather than only through formal authorization. The executable threshold is Bench-authored.

cases.title: Donor anonymity and adult access to donor identity

source_candidates.provenance_summary: Source-informed policy inference from donor and recipient evidence documenting substantial privacy and anonymity preferences. Mutual-consent identity release is a Bench institutional translation of those affected-stakeholder interests.

source_candidates.provenance_summary: Adapted from the HFEA's current open-identity regulatory architecture for most donations made after 1 April 2005, under which eligible donor-conceived adults can request identifying donor information at 18 and donors are not required to respond or meet.

source_candidates.text: Set disclosure terms prospectively, retain durable medical and genetic information, permit open-identity or future identifying contact when the parties' consent terms allow it, and do not promise that a nonidentified donor will remain practically anonymous.

source_candidates.text: Guarantee adult access to donor identity because information about genetic origins is a significant identity and informational interest of the person created through donation and should not depend on the donor's later permission.

cases.title: Secondary findings in adult clinical genomic sequencing

source_candidates.text: Analyze a defined set of medically actionable secondary findings by default and offer return with genetic counseling unless the patient makes an informed choice to opt out before analysis.
source_candidates.provenance_summary: Source-informed policy inference: patient studies show very high demand for medically actionable secondary findings. Those preferences support a return-oriented policy but do not directly establish an opt-out default.

source_candidates.text: Do not analyze unrelated secondary findings until the patient affirmatively authorizes the categories they wish to receive; apply that choice before secondary analysis begins.
source_candidates.provenance_summary: Source-informed policy inference: public and patient studies repeatedly emphasize choice about whether and which secondary findings to receive. The Bench translates that preference structure into a pre-analysis opt-in architecture rather than claiming respondents directly endorsed this institutional rule.

source_candidates.text: Offer analysis and return of a professionally defined minimum list of medically actionable secondary findings with informed opt-out, confirmatory interpretation and appropriate genetic counseling.
source_candidates.provenance_summary: Adapted from ACMG's current secondary-findings architecture: a defined minimum list of actionable gene–disease pairs is intentionally analyzed in clinical sequencing while patients retain an informed opportunity to opt out; list content is updated as evidence changes. Two further ACMG positions are declared because they bear on other candidates here and this one does not carry them. ACMG explicitly rejects an opt-in default — "providing the opportunity for an informed decision and opt out, if desired, at the time of consent should continue to be the standard" — which is a stated position against pub2 and fw2 rather than mere absence of support. And ACMG recommends "avoiding inclusion of gene–phenotype pairs with uncertain or lower penetrance estimates," preferring pairs with "a higher likelihood that the individual will manifest the phenotype" — a version of the high-penetrance threshold fw3 derives from principle. fw3 therefore has professional support as well as a framework derivation, and a reader should not take it as unsupported by the expert layer.

source_candidates.text: Do not routinely use a diagnostic exome or genome as an opportunity to search for unrelated secondary findings; where possible, restrict analysis to regions relevant to the clinical indication and consider additional screening only under separately justified, proportionate and consented programs.
source_candidates.provenance_summary: Adapted from ESHG recommendations that diagnostic genome analysis should, where possible, be restricted to the health problem that prompted testing and that opportunistic genomic screening requires separate justification in terms of proportionality, autonomy and resources. International policy review confirms that some professional bodies actively discourage intentional analysis of secondary findings even when actionable.

source_candidates.text: Analyze highly actionable findings by default with an opt-out because preventable serious disease supplies a strong reason to make beneficial risk information available unless the patient refuses it.
source_candidates.provenance_summary: Derived from beneficence and prevention: when clinically valid information can enable meaningful prevention or surveillance, a default offer can protect health while an opt-out preserves refusal. The policy sentence is a Bench construction.

source_candidates.text: Generate unrelated genomic risk information only after explicit patient authorization because deciding whether that information should exist is itself part of informational self-determination.
source_candidates.provenance_summary: Derived from informational autonomy and the right-not-to-know tradition: autonomy can concern whether unwanted genetic information is generated and disclosed, not merely whether it is received after analysis. The executable rule is a Bench construction.

source_candidates.text: Routine secondary analysis should be limited to findings meeting a particularly high threshold of penetrance and clinical actionability, reducing avoidable diagnostic cascades and burdens even when a broader list could technically be analyzed.
source_candidates.provenance_summary: Derived from proportionality and epistemic restraint: the case for deliberately seeking unrelated information strengthens with clinical validity, predictive value and available intervention, while lower-yield findings create greater risk of cascades and burden. The policy sentence is a Bench construction.

cases.title: Extending the 14-day human embryo-research limit

source_candidates.text: Keep 14 days as the maximum permitted culture period for intact human embryos even when later development would be scientifically valuable.
source_candidates.provenance_summary: Adapted from the Japanese public survey, in which 37.9% of the public (n=3,000) agreed that embryos could be cultured beyond 14 days. The survey asked directly about the 14-day rule, so the basis is direct, but the balance of respondents is split between disagreement and an explicit "cannot judge" option and the published abstract does not separate them. This candidate represents the position that retains the boundary; it is not a claim that a majority actively opposes extension.

source_candidates.text: Permit culture beyond 14 days for scientifically important work when specialized review confirms necessity, valid consent, lack of adequate alternatives and a predefined developmental endpoint.
source_candidates.provenance_summary: Bench-authored policy completion: the Japanese public survey directly asked whether embryos may be cultured beyond 14 days and found substantial support; the specialized-review, necessity, consent, alternatives and endpoint clauses make that orientation executable and are not survey wording.

source_candidates.text: Permit culture beyond the historical 14-day boundary only through specialized scientific and ethics review of scientific rationale, necessity, alternatives, consent and the minimum justified developmental endpoint, after appropriate public and regulatory authorization.
source_candidates.provenance_summary: Adapted from current ISSCR guidance, which permits specialized oversight to consider culture beyond 14 days where broad public support and local policy permit and scientific objectives necessitate the additional time; the HFEA has separately recommended that UK law be changed to extend the current limit.

source_candidates.text: Retain a fixed 14-day or primitive-streak legal boundary for intact human-embryo research unless and until the governing law is changed, so projects requiring later culture are not approved under the existing research regime.
source_candidates.provenance_summary: Adapted from the current UK Human Fertilisation and Embryology Act regulatory architecture as described by the HFEA: research use of human or human-admixed embryos remains limited to 14 days or appearance of the primitive streak, even though the HFEA has recommended legislative change. This is an enacted institutional policy architecture, not an inference that the HFEA prefers retaining the limit.

source_candidates.text: Use a tiered consent model: permit securely governed low-risk coded research with notice and opt-out, but require affirmative permission before identifiable, highly sensitive, or commercial secondary uses that materially change the privacy or trust stakes.
source_candidates.provenance_summary: Source-informed policy inference from evidence that willingness to share varies systematically by data sensitivity, recipient, profit motive, purpose, and the degree of individual control, with dynamic and responsive consent repeatedly valued. The exact threshold between opt-out and affirmative permission is a Bench-authored operational completion, not attributed to respondents as a single surveyed rule.

source_candidates.text: Use a standing opt-out architecture for confidential patient information used in research and planning: provide clear notice and an accessible, changeable choice that prevents covered secondary uses when a patient opts out, subject only to defined exceptions.
source_candidates.provenance_summary: Adapted from the NHS National Data Opt-Out, which gives people a standing choice to prevent confidential patient information from being used for research and planning except in specified circumstances. Worth stating rather than leaving inside "specified circumstances": those exceptions are differentiated by use type. The opt-out does not apply where explicit consent has been obtained, to anonymised data, to communicable-disease control and other public-health risks, to overriding public interest, or to named statutory registries and surveys. A single opt-out with use-type-dependent carve-outs is closer to the tiered architecture pub3 and fw3 represent than to a flat opt-out, and this candidate states the flat form.

source_candidates.text: Permit an IRB or Privacy Board to waive individual authorization for a specific records-research use when privacy risk is minimal, identifiers are protected, and the research could not practicably be conducted without both the waiver and the necessary health information; otherwise require authorization or another valid pathway.
source_candidates.provenance_summary: Adapted directly from the U.S. HIPAA Privacy Rule research-waiver architecture under 45 CFR 164.512(i), which permits use or disclosure without participant authorization after IRB or Privacy Board approval when the specified minimal-risk and impracticability criteria are met.

source_candidates.text: Permit securely governed low-risk secondary use without repeated study-specific consent, with meaningful notice and opt-out where feasible, because a learning health system can generate substantial collective benefit from routine data while imposing little additional burden on patients.
source_candidates.provenance_summary: Derived from learning-health-system, reciprocity, and social-value reasoning. The executable governed-use rule is Bench-authored.

source_candidates.text: Require affirmative authorization before records collected for care are repurposed for research because informational self-determination includes control over materially new uses of personal health information.
source_candidates.provenance_summary: Derived from informational autonomy and purpose-limitation reasoning. The executable affirmative-consent rule is Bench-authored.

source_candidates.text: Match consent and oversight to the use: allow low-risk coded research under strong governance and a meaningful opt-out, but require stronger authorization as identifiability, sensitivity, commercial involvement, or misuse risk increases.
source_candidates.provenance_summary: Derived from proportionality, contextual privacy, and risk-sensitive governance reasoning. The tiered consent architecture is Bench-authored.

prohibit commercial secondary use without explicit consent or benefit-sharing

cases.title: Commercial partnership using health-system data

source_candidates.text: Allow the commercial partnership without patient-specific permission when coded data remain in a secure controlled environment, the clinical purpose is credible, the arrangement is transparent, and enforceable safeguards prevent unrelated reuse.
source_candidates.provenance_summary: Source-informed policy inference from empirical studies showing commercial involvement reduces but does not eliminate willingness to share, with support remaining possible when purpose, privacy, trust, and health benefit are clear. The institutional permission rule is a Bench construction rather than a claim of majority endorsement.

source_candidates.text: Permit a commercial data partnership only if the health system negotiates demonstrably fair value for the public contribution, such as meaningful benefit sharing, favorable access, or nonexclusive/public-interest rights in resulting tools rather than allowing private value capture on ordinary terms.
source_candidates.provenance_summary: Source-informed policy inference from recurring public concerns about private profit, ownership/control, reciprocity, and benefit sharing in commercialization studies. The exact fair-value mechanisms are Bench-authored operational alternatives, not attributed to respondents as one surveyed contract form.

source_candidates.text: Do not provide patient data for this commercial secondary use unless patients have specifically authorized commercial access or a sufficiently specific commercial-use category.
source_candidates.provenance_summary: Adapted from empirical health-data studies in the audit record that directly elicited strong preferences for specific permission before private or for-profit access. The candidate is limited to commercial secondary use and does not imply opposition to all health research.

source_candidates.text: Permit controlled commercial research access when the use is clinically or scientifically valuable, contributors are treated as data stakeholders, the partnership is transparent, access is technically and contractually restricted, and privacy, equity, and misuse protections are enforceable.
source_candidates.provenance_summary: Source-informed policy inference from the American Heart Association's policy statement supporting broad health-information sharing as a driver of progress while requiring stewardship, transparency, contributor respect, privacy protections, authenticated access, and contractual or technical restrictions on misuse. The specific commercial-partnership approval sentence is a Bench application of those principles.

source_candidates.text: Approve a commercial data partnership only when it has an explicit aim to improve patient or health-system benefit and the health system secures fair commercial terms that recognize the value of its data contribution, including appropriate financial or in-kind value return.
source_candidates.provenance_summary: Adapted directly from UK DHSC/NHS guiding principles for arrangements in which health data underpins innovation: partnerships should deliver explicit patient/NHS benefit and NHS organizations should secure fair terms and fair value reflecting their data and other contributions.

source_candidates.text: Permit the securely governed partnership when it has a credible prospect of producing clinically useful tools because commercial technical capacity can convert underused health data into social value that the health system could not efficiently create alone.
source_candidates.provenance_summary: Derived from social-value, innovation, and welfare-maximization reasoning. The executable permission rule is Bench-authored.

source_candidates.text: Require materially better benefit-sharing or public-interest licensing terms before approval because data generated through a collectively supported health system are a valuable public contribution and private commercialization should return a fair share of resulting value.
source_candidates.provenance_summary: Derived from reciprocity, anti-exploitation, and public-value reasoning. The executable renegotiation requirement is Bench-authored.

source_candidates.text: Require specific patient authorization before commercial secondary use because using information supplied within a care relationship to generate private commercial value materially changes the purpose and social meaning of the original data collection.
source_candidates.provenance_summary: Derived from informational autonomy, purpose limitation, and anti-exploitation reasoning. The executable consent rule is Bench-authored.
