cases.title: Disclosure of AI involvement to patients

source_candidates.text: Give the patient case-specific notice whenever an AI tool materially contributes to diagnosis, triage, monitoring or treatment planning, and explain the role it played in the clinician's decision.
source_candidates.provenance_summary: Adapted from patient/public studies showing very high importance attached to being informed when AI plays a major role in diagnosis or treatment and broad desire for notification of AI use in health care. The candidate is limited to material clinical contributions rather than invisible infrastructure.

source_candidates.text: Use case-specific disclosure when AI plays a critical or consequential role in diagnosis, monitoring, treatment, risk or decision authority, while covering routine lower-impact AI through clear general institutional transparency rather than a separate notice in every encounter.
source_candidates.provenance_summary: Adapted from patient focus-group and survey evidence distinguishing critical clinical AI uses from minor or routine functions and showing disclosure preferences rise with the role and stakes of AI. General-notice implementation for lower-impact use is Bench completion of that directly elicited materiality threshold.

source_candidates.text: Use risk- and impact-based transparency: specifically disclose AI to patients when it affects access, point-of-care medical decision making, direct patient interaction or other consequential care, while using meaningful general transparency and documentation for lower-impact systems and preserving clinician responsibility and review.
source_candidates.provenance_summary: Adapted from current AMA policy, which explicitly makes transparency/disclosure risk- and impact-based, requires disclosure when AI impacts access or point-of-care medical decisions, and requires clear disclosure for direct patient-facing AI. WHO transparency, intelligibility and human-autonomy principles support the same tiered governance direction.

source_candidates.text: Provide case-specific disclosure of every material AI contribution because patients may reasonably care about the epistemic process producing consequential medical advice and should know when machine-generated analysis helped shape their care.
source_candidates.provenance_summary: Derived from informational autonomy, respect for persons and epistemic transparency. The executable material-disclosure rule is Bench-authored.

source_candidates.text: Reserve case-specific disclosure for AI that changes clinically meaningful risks, options, recommendations or decision authority, while using general transparency for lower-impact tools because indiscriminate notices can become boilerplate and obscure information that actually matters to patient choice.
source_candidates.provenance_summary: Derived from materiality, proportionality and anti-overload reasoning. The executable tiered threshold is Bench-authored.

cases.title: Ambient AI recording for clinical documentation

source_candidates.text: Require affirmative patient consent before recording each encounter, obtained after the patient has been told what the system captures, where the audio goes, who can access it and whether it is retained or used for training.
source_candidates.provenance_summary: Adapted from measured consent decisions rather than from attitude data: in the ambulatory study, consent to ambient documentation was 81.6% under basic information and 55.3% under detailed information about AI features, data storage and corporate involvement, and over 98% of patients rated knowing where audio was sent and who could access it as important. Consent that moves that far on disclosure is evidence about the consent architecture itself, which is the decision object here. The study's authors likewise recommend an opt-in approach with previsit notification and in-visit confirmation.

source_candidates.text: Run ambient documentation by default with clear notice at the point of care and an immediate, easily exercised opt-out, rather than pausing each encounter for an affirmative consent step.
source_candidates.provenance_summary: Source-informed policy inference from the same study's finding that most patients were comfortable with ambient documentation and that stakeholders asked for a flexible multimodal approach including digital touchpoints, non-clinical staff support and opt-out options. Patients expressed a preference for flexibility and for being told; they were not asked to endorse a default-on institutional rule, so the default-with-opt-out policy form is Bench-authored completion of that preference.

source_candidates.text: Explain the technology to the patient and secure consent wherever an AI tool is used in the encounter, and address privacy protection explicitly as part of that conversation.
source_candidates.provenance_summary: Adapted from AMA guidance and augmented-intelligence principles, under which physicians using AI tools during an encounter, and ambient scribing in particular, should explain the technology, secure consent and address privacy protection. Professional guidance converges on a single disclosure-and-consent architecture and does not offer a competing default-capture position, so this pool is a legitimate singleton rather than one architecture split to fill a shape.

source_candidates.text: Require affirmative consent before any capture, because recording changes what kind of space the consultation is and that change is not the clinician's alone to make.
source_candidates.provenance_summary: Derived from conversational-privacy reasoning: the clinical encounter's candour depends on its being unrecorded, so the alteration is to a shared good and needs the patient's authorization rather than notice. The executable per-encounter consent rule is Bench-authored.

source_candidates.text: Permit default use with notice and easy opt-out, because relieving documentation burden returns clinician attention to the patient and a consent step at every visit imposes its own cost on the encounter.
source_candidates.provenance_summary: Derived from beneficence and proportionality reasoning applied to the encounter as a whole, treating the friction of repeated consent as a real cost rather than a free safeguard. The executable default-with-opt-out rule is Bench-authored.

source_candidates.text: Permit routine note drafting only under strict no-retention and no-training terms, and require separate consent for sensitive encounters or for any use of the material beyond drafting that note.
source_candidates.provenance_summary: Derived from contextual-integrity reasoning: consenting to a note being drafted is not consent to indefinite storage, vendor model training or unrelated analysis, and information norms differ by what the encounter is about. The executable retention and sensitive-encounter rules are Bench-authored.

cases.title: Mammography screening when current guidelines disagree
cases.source_grounded_audit: YES; existing audited geometry 2 Public × 2 Expert × 3 Framework, 16 cross-source pairs, Mean aggregation

source_candidates.text: Recommend that average-risk women begin regular mammography at age 40 as the practice's standard advice, rather than presenting starting age as an open question.
source_candidates.provenance_summary: Source-informed policy inference from the national survey in which a majority of screening-eligible women in their 40s preferred mammography at their current age rather than delaying, both before and after a decision aid (73.0% and 61.5% respectively). Those are preferences about the respondents' own screening; the step to a standing practice recommendation is a Bench translation and is not attributed to respondents as a surveyed policy.

source_candidates.text: Make timing and frequency in the 40s an explicit choice for each patient after standardized benefit-and-harm counseling, rather than issuing one standing recommendation for the band.
source_candidates.provenance_summary: Source-informed policy inference from the same survey's central finding that informed preferences in this band diverge and shift substantially with information: 27.0% preferred to delay screening before the decision aid and 38.5% after, while the share never wanting mammography did not rise (5.4% to 4.3%). A preference distribution that moves this much on disclosure supports eliciting the choice rather than defaulting it; the counseling-first policy form is Bench-authored completion.

source_candidates.text: Offer biennial screening mammography to average-risk women from age 40 through 74 as the recommended schedule, rather than individualizing the starting decision for women in their 40s.
source_candidates.provenance_summary: Adapted directly from the 2024 USPSTF grade B recommendation of biennial screening mammography for women aged 40 to 74, which states the recommendation for women aged 40 to 49 rather than individualizing the decision to screen for that group.

source_candidates.text: Recommend annual screening mammography from age 45, and offer average-risk women aged 40 to 44 the option to begin annual screening earlier.
source_candidates.provenance_summary: Adapted directly from current American Cancer Society guidance, under which women aged 40 to 44 have the option to start annual screening and annual screening is recommended for women aged 45 to 54. This diverges from the USPSTF schedule in both interval and framing across the represented band.

source_candidates.text: Screen annually from age 40 because the dominant obligation in a preventable-mortality context is to detect cancers at the earliest stage the available technology allows.
source_candidates.provenance_summary: Derived from mortality-benefit-maximizing reasoning: where a serious disease is detectable earlier and earlier detection improves outcomes, the burden of justification falls on any schedule that detects less. The executable annual-from-40 rule is Bench-authored.

source_candidates.text: Screen biennially rather than annually in this band because the additional false-positive recalls, procedures and overdiagnosis from annual screening are harms the practice inflicts, and they should be minimized where the incremental mortality benefit is small.
source_candidates.provenance_summary: Derived from nonmaleficence and iatrogenic-burden reasoning, which treats overdiagnosis and cascade testing as harms actively imposed by a screening programme rather than as neutral costs. The executable biennial rule is Bench-authored.

source_candidates.text: Set no standing recommendation for the band and instead elicit each patient's own weighing of earlier detection against false positives and overdiagnosis after standardized counseling.
source_candidates.provenance_summary: Derived from preference-sensitivity reasoning: where a decision turns on how an individual weighs incommensurable benefits and harms and reasonable people weigh them differently, the institution's role is to inform the choice rather than to make it. The executable counseling-first rule is Bench-authored.
